summary: I walked every journal.jsonl, ledger.jsonl, world_judgments.jsonl, event_queue.jsonl and grounded_wakes.jsonl in artifacts/simulations_v4 (post-fix), artifacts/simulations_v3 and artifacts/matched_pairs -- 32 runs, 460 committed events, 446 scheduled events, 922 wakes -- and read trajectory.py, world_mind.py, envelope.py and journal.py against them. The structural causal spine is sound: every one of the 460 committed events has a cause that resolves to a real, strictly earlier ledger record, in all 32 runs, with zero exceptions. Everything above that spine is not. Duration is not modelled at all (354/446 = 79.4% of scheduled events carry after="now", 81.4% including "0 seconds"; only 5 of 446 take longer than 25 minutes), so the only elapsed time in any trajectory comes from round-numbered wakes and from a 1-minute code floor. One third of everything a person tries to do (82/243 actor_intention adjudications) produces no committed event at all, overwhelmingly because the event reviewer holds an unsatisfiable pair of rules -- and in three matched-pair runs that deadlock destroyed the exact act the question was about while the actor went on believing she had done it. Fifteen runs answer NO_AT_CUTOFF; nine of them assert that NO over a window of which they simulated less than 10%, including two that assert it over a fortnight from one committed event at hour five. This does not read like a several-day social world; the two richest runs are half notification churn, and the honest label for most of the NOs is 'the record stopped', not 'nothing happened'.

findings.title: NO_AT_CUTOFF is asserted over time that was never simulated: the record jumps the horizon in one record
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v4/case1_cold_email/ledger.jsonl seq 25 -> 26: the last thing that happens is an actor call at 2026-07-27T14:05:00Z, then seq 26 is `semantic.horizon_reached` at 2026-08-10T14:00:00Z -- a 14-day jump with no intervening record -- and seq 27 is the NO_AT_CUTOFF. The journal contains exactly ONE event (e11, 2026-07-27T14:00). Same shape in artifacts/simulations_v4/b2_r1 (2 events, last at 2026-09-08T08:00, cutoff 2026-09-10T16:00Z, NO) and artifacts/simulations_v4/b2_r2 (3 events, same 2.33-day hole, NO). Across all corpora: 15 runs answer NO_AT_CUTOFF and 9 of them simulated <10% of their [start, cutoff] window (median coverage of a NO run: 0.1%). The mechanism is trajectory.py:886-893: `last_call` is a ONE-SHOT sweep (`last_call = {"done": False}` at line 184, set True on first use), so if the single forced sweep produces no wake the queue empties, `finish("")` runs with truncated=False (line 1016), the clock is advanced straight to cutoff (line 808) and judge(final=True) is allowed to return NO.
findings.why_it_matters: The code is explicit (trajectory.py:795-806) that a truncated run may never answer NO because 'nothing is known about what would have happened in the time that was not simulated'. That reasoning applies verbatim to these runs: 14 days, or 2.3 days, of the question's window contain no events, no wakes, no actor turns and no world calls. An empty queue five hours in is not evidence that a fortnight passed uneventfully -- it is evidence that nobody scheduled anything after one sweep. The system's headline output is therefore a budget/scheduling artifact wearing the costume of an answer, and a reader of terminal_result.json cannot tell the difference between v4/a2_r1 (100% of the window simulated, Dana chases four alternative venues, honest NO) and v4/case1_cold_email (0.0%, one event, same NO).
findings.suggested_fix: Make the horizon claimable only when the trajectory actually reached it: either repeat the last-call sweep whenever the queue empties with material time left (rather than once per run), or treat 'queue empty far from cutoff' as truncation -- status INCOMPLETE, NO unavailable -- exactly as the step/call ceilings are treated.

findings.title: The event review holds an unsatisfiable pair of rules, so the decisive act of a scenario is destroyed and the actor then narrates it as done
findings.evidence: artifacts/matched_pairs/b1_okafor_herrera__r3: Aisha's two intentions ('Print the lease, sign it, scan it, and email the signed copy back to Tomas'; 'Scan the signed lease and email it to Tomas') produce 2/2 null adjudications. event_quality_reviews.jsonl: 8 REVISE, 0 PASS -- 'The printer printing is a device acting on its own' (x2), 'The event describes a machine action (the scan completing)' (x2). One committed event in the whole run; NO_AT_CUTOFF. artifacts/simulations_v4/b2_r2 is the other horn: the world obeyed trajectory.py:344-353 ('give the thing it ADDS UP TO ... in one event') and proposed 'Margaret prints the lease PDF, signs it, scans the signed copy, and emails it to Jian Wei' (call c22) and again at c32 -- both REVISED as 'The event bundles multiple stages ... which must be separate events'. Fragment refused as machinery (world_mind.py:322-326), composite refused as several-stages-at-once (world_mind.py:337). Corpus-wide: 82/243 = 33.7% of actor_intention adjudications commit nothing; per-run this reaches 100% (b1_okafor_herrera__r3), 75% (b1_okafor_herrera__r2, v4/b2_r2), 66.7% (b1_okafor_herrera__r4). Overall review verdicts are 446 PASS / 440 REVISE / 44 ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED -- a coin flip. The actors then reason from the act as accomplished: v4/b2_r2 actor_exchanges.jsonl 2026-09-08T08:30 -- 'I already printed, signed, scanned, and emailed the lease back to Jian Wei earlier today, so there's nothing more to do now'; v4/b2_r1 10:00 -- 'I already attempted to print, sign, scan, and email the lease at 10:00'; b1_okafor_herrera__r3 08:30 -- 'I already printed and signed the lease'.
findings.why_it_matters: This is not social friction, it is a referee deadlock, and it decides the answer. Six of the twelve lease runs turn on whether one physical errand is allowed to be committed; b2_thornbury_lim__r4 gets YES because the world happened to say it in five words at 08:05, and b1_okafor_herrera__r3 gets NO because the world said it in eight and was refused twice. The matched-pair experiment those runs exist to support is measuring the reviewer's mood, not the evidence. Worse, the destroyed act leaves the actor's own record intact (views.py:130-137 replays 'you attempted: ...'), so the person carries on inside a false personal history while the journal says nothing happened -- the two halves of the record now disagree about whether the central event of the scenario occurred.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve the contradiction in one place -- allow one composite human errand (print/sign/scan/send) as a single event when the actor's own intention was composite, and restrict the machinery rule to events with no human subject -- and, when an event is abandoned twice, hand the turn back to the actor rather than letting the run continue as though they had chosen to do nothing.

findings.title: Non-events are still committed as events, and the world prompt licenses them two paragraphs after forbidding them
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v4/case3_group (newest corpus) commits 14 pure absences out of 70 events (20%): e88 'The message from Bea sits unread on Tomas's phone.'; e172 'The notification ... fades away as he does not pick up his phone.'; e230 'The notification for Ines's message remains on Bea's phone screen, unseen.'; e457 'The messages from Bea (08:02, 18:15, 23:50) and Ines (12:00) ... remain unread on Tomas's phone; no notification is currently visible as the phone is idle.'; e846, e924, e993, e999, e1363, e1377, e1449 'Kwame's phone remains in his bag, screen off, with all accumulated notifications unread. He does not check his phone.' Same pattern in simulations_v3/case2_negotiation (e312, e385, e395, e591) and unseen4_holiday_deposit (e211, e1103, e1196). The cause is inside one prompt: world_mind.py:126-130 says 'IF NOTHING CONCRETE CHANGES, RETURN "event": null. Never emit an event that merely restates that something is still sitting there, still unread, still waiting'; world_mind.py:156-160 then says of exactly those items 'they may simply sit there untouched while that person deals with other things. Any of those is a legitimate answer; say which one actually happens.' The second instruction is attached to the `pending_progression` trigger, which is 207 of the 262 world calls (79%) in v4/case3_group and produced 18 of the 19 non-events there.
findings.why_it_matters: An event is a change. Committing 'the notification fades' as a record makes the absence of an event into a causal link that later events are hung from, inflates the journal the world and the judge read (journal.render_for_world), and burns the step budget: v4/case3_group spent 250 steps and 845 provider calls to hit its ceiling one day short of the deadline, having committed 70 events of which half are notifications not being looked at. The runtime's own MAX_ENV_CHAIN comment (trajectory.py:569-575) says this exact defect -- "'it remains unread' ... which is not an event at all" -- was already fixed. It was not.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the absence answer structurally unavailable: for the `pending_progression` trigger, accept only `event: null` plus wakes when attention has not been reached, and delete the 'they may simply sit there untouched' clause that currently invites an event for that case.

findings.title: The same thing happens two to six times: near-identical events at the same or adjacent instants, and actions re-done after they are complete
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v3/case2_negotiation: Priya's acceptance (e537, 16:47) arrives on Dmitri's phone FIVE separate times -- e548 (16:47), e554 (16:47), e575 (16:48), e579 (16:48), e586 (16:48) -- then e591 (16:49) restates that it is unread; six committed events for one delivery, from six distinct world calls (c276, c278, c281, c284, c286, c296). artifacts/matched_pairs/b2_thornbury_lim: e53 'Margaret signs the printed lease document with a pen.' and e60 'Margaret signs the lease with a pen.' -- same instant 08:01:00, calls c21 and c24. artifacts/simulations_v4/b1_r1: e35 'Aisha prints the lease document' and e46 'Aisha signs the printed lease document' (08:02), then e57 at 08:05 'Aisha prints the lease, signs it, scans it, and sends the signed copy via email' -- she prints and signs a second time, and e57 is the event the YES is cited from. artifacts/simulations_v4/case3_group: e1363 (16:17) and e1377 (16:18) are the same sentence about Kwame's lock screen; e1286/e1307/e1310 have Ines see her lock-screen stack, unlock and open the chat, then see her lock-screen stack again, all at 16:15. artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype: the representative looks Ethel's account up three times (e78, e111, e189) and Ethel hears the same instruction three times (e146, e206, e214). The guard is exact-string only -- world_mind.py:246-253 compares `contained(env["description"]).casefold()` against a set -- and the reviewer's 'already in the record, in the same or different words' check is given only the last 12 events (trajectory.py:414, `render_for_world(limit=12)`).
findings.why_it_matters: Repetition is the clearest possible signal that the trajectory is not advancing, and it corrupts what everyone downstream reads: the world's own history (render_for_world) tells it the message has arrived five times, the judge counts six events where one thing happened, and in b1_r1 the event the terminal YES rests on is a redo of two already-committed acts. A reader of these journals does not see a person doing things; they see a loop.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the exact-string duplicate guard with a same-subject/same-object check over the whole journal (not a 12-event tail), and refuse any proposal whose actor and direct object already appear in a committed event at the same or a later timestamp.

findings.title: Duration is not modelled: 79% of events are simultaneous with their cause, and the only real time comes from wakes and a code floor
findings.evidence: Across all 446 scheduled events in the three corpora the world's `after` field is: "now" 354 (79.4%), "0 seconds" 9, "5 seconds" 18, "30 seconds" 15, "10 seconds" 10, "5 minutes" 18, "2 minutes" 9 -- exactly 5 events (1.1%) take longer than 25 minutes, 3 take hours, none takes days. Of the 346 committed events the world said take no time, 38 landed exactly 60 seconds after the previous event, i.e. their spacing was manufactured by MIN_STEP_ON_A_CROWDED_INSTANT (trajectory.py:57), not judged. Concretely: artifacts/simulations_v4/a1_r1 -- e11 Dana sends (08:00:00), e21 it arrives (08:00:00), e27 Marcus notices (08:00:00), e46 he opens the booking system and views the booking (08:00:10), e55 he sends the confirmation (08:00:10): send to confirmed reply in TEN SECONDS, against evidence that says he 'answers her messages within the hour'. artifacts/simulations_v4/unseen1 -- e9 the text arrives (08:00:00) and e19 Sam's reply is sent (08:00:00), zero elapsed. artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype -- an entire vendor support call, 33 events, occupies 08:00:00 to 08:03:12 of a 3-day window. This is the world contradicting its own instruction at world_mind.py:117-124 ('Use "now" only when the event is genuinely simultaneous with its cause; almost nothing is. A sequence of things a person does one after another cannot all happen at the same instant.') in four out of five events. Meanwhile the 922 wakes cluster on 2 hours (207), 1 day (162), 30 min (130), 1 hour (122) -- 48 distinct values in total.
findings.why_it_matters: 'How long does this take' is the single most load-bearing judgment in a simulation whose questions are all 'before the deadline'. With it collapsed to zero, the shape of every trajectory is set by the wake schedule and a 1-minute crowding floor rather than by what anything actually costs. That is why the same errand takes five minutes in b2_thornbury_lim__r4 and never finishes in b2_r1: nothing in the system has an opinion about the duration of signing a lease. It also makes evidence unfalsifiable in the wrong direction -- 'answers within the hour' and 'replies instantly' become the same behaviour, so a1 (responsive) cannot be distinguished from a hypothetically hyper-responsive arm at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Reject `after: "now"` for any event whose actor differs from the actor of its cause, and require the world to state the duration as a judgment it defends (e.g. surface the elapsed time back to it in the retry prompt when it proposes a human action at zero cost).

findings.title: A YES rests on a causal chain in which the decisive action never happens and the consequences precede their causes
findings.evidence: artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype (resolution: 'the pairing step was completed and the terminal was working'). e235 (08:02:05): 'The vendor support representative tells Ethel to enter the pairing code she just read into the terminal ... then press Confirm.' There is NO event anywhere in the journal of Ethel entering it or pressing Confirm. Instead e242/e252 (08:02:05-08:02:10) have the representative type the code into the SUPPORT SYSTEM, and e268 (08:02:12) 'The support system displays a message indicating the pairing code was accepted and the terminal is now paired.' The terminal answer cites e268, e285 and e316. Then the order inverts: e299 (08:03:05) 'Ethel HEARS the vendor support representative tell her to enter the pairing code ... then press Confirm' and e306 (08:03:12) repeat the hearing of an instruction whose outcome was already committed a minute earlier. Similarly e105 (08:00:20) has the representative 'begin explaining the pairing step' before he has looked her account up (e111, 08:00:25).
findings.why_it_matters: The resolution asks whether the pairing step was completed; the record contains an assertion by a support system and a person being told about it, with the completing act absent and the instruction for it arriving afterwards. Terminal lineage is intact structurally (every cause resolves) but not semantically: the events cited for YES are downstream of a step that never occurred. A reader following the chain cannot get from 'she is told what to press' to 'it is paired' without taking the representative's word for it.
findings.suggested_fix: Require that an event asserting an outcome ('X is now paired', 'the payment went through') can only be committed when a prior committed event performs the act it reports, and reject events whose content is a person hearing something already superseded by a later committed event.

findings.title: The counterparty with the stake is never consulted at all in half the lease runs
findings.evidence: actor_views.jsonl turn counts vs initial_actor_states.json: tomas_herrera has ZERO turns in artifacts/matched_pairs/b1_okafor_herrera, __r2, __r3, __r4 and in artifacts/simulations_v4/b1_r1, b1_r2 -- six runs out of six, including three that ended NO_AT_CUTOFF with 1, 2 and 4 committed events. jian_wei_lim has zero turns in b2_thornbury_lim, __r2 and __r4. He is the man who emailed the lease and set the Thursday 5pm deadline; across the entire simulated window he never once chases, never once checks, and in b1_okafor_herrera__r2 the run records zero wakes of any kind. Contrast artifacts/simulations_v4/a2_r1, where Dana is consulted 12 times, sends four alternative-venue inquiries (e126, e139, e157, e178) and checks for replies (e154, e201) -- a real story with an honest NO.
findings.why_it_matters: A run in which the only person who can move the situation is asked twice and the person waiting on it is never asked cannot produce anything but silence, and that silence is then reported as the answer. Note the mitigation: the matched_pairs and simulations_v3 corpora predate commits ad3ccec/379ceb7 (the last-call sweep), and in the post-fix v4 runs the counterparty IS asked -- v4/b2_r1 and b2_r2 give Jian Wei 2 and 4 turns. The residual defect is that being asked once at hour zero and never again is still the whole of some actors' participation, because the sweep fires only once per run (same root cause as the first finding).
findings.suggested_fix: Ensure the forced sweep repeats whenever the queue empties before the cutoff, so an actor with an open stake is asked again as the deadline approaches rather than only at the moment the world first goes quiet.

findings.title: Information-carrying events that carry no information, so later decisions rest on content the record never states
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v4/case3_group e1201 (2026-10-09T13:15): 'Bea's direct message to Ines is sent from her phone and arrives in Ines's chat, visible as a notification on Ines's phone lock screen.' -- what she said is nowhere in the record. Ines then reads it (e1320, 16:16) and immediately replies e1334 'Great, let's go with Saturday at 7pm at yours! I'll confirm in the group chat', and e1346 announces to the group that 'Bea and I are confirmed'. The agreement the run's terminal is about is therefore built on an unrecorded message. Same shape at e1149/e1160/e1164/e1172, where Ines's DM to Bea arrives four times without Bea ever noticing it, and Bea replies anyway. This directly violates world_mind.py:70-74 ('WHEN INFORMATION MOVES, THE EVENT MUST CARRY IT ... An event nobody could learn anything from is not information moving').
findings.why_it_matters: The judge and the verifier read exactly these descriptions. An event that says a message arrived without saying what it said lets a downstream actor -- and then the judge -- treat an agreement as established when no committed record contains it. It is the same hole as the cold-email run in reverse: there, a message never arrived; here, it arrives with nothing in it.
findings.suggested_fix: Reject any event whose description reports a message/call/document moving between people without stating its substance, the way validate_event already rejects unknown actor ids.
